title: The Impact of COVID-19 on African American Dental Students’ Self-Confidence in Implementing Specific Clinical Treatments
content: Background/Objectives: Few studies have examined the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on the clinical readiness of dental students in the provision of care. This study examined whether dental students who graduated during the pre-pandemic period would have higher self-reported clinical skills confidence than those who graduated during the post-pandemic period. Methods: A cross-sectional online survey was sent to dental graduates from two Historically Black Colleges and Universities in the United States. The questionnaire included a validated 40-item instrument to measure self-reported confidence in clinical procedures and questions about relevant demographic variables. Results: In fixed prosthodontics, confidence decreased significantly for tooth preparation, impressions, try-in of ceramic-fused-to-metal restorations, and cementation of fixed prostheses (p< 0.05). Confidence also declined for diagnostic and periodontal procedures, including mucogingival anomaly diagnosis, surgical elimination of periodontal pockets, and management of traumatic dental contacts (p< 0.05). The largest decline was seen in the diagnosis and conservative treatment of oroantral communications and fistulas. Particularly of clinical and statistical importance, there were significant reductions in self-confidence in the ability to perform tooth extractions and minor oral surgery in medically compromised patients, tooth extractions with separation of roots, and diagnosis and therapy of acute and chronic dental infections (p< 0.05). Conclusions: The findings provide further evidence of the adverse effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on the African American dental workforce. Strategies to address the educational deficiencies of dental students who graduated during the pandemic era need to be developed and implemented.
